answers.text: Instruction: 'From the supplier email, always return exactly three lines, in order: Date: <delivery date>; Item: <item and quantity>; Change: <difference from the original order, or "no change">.' If a field isn't in the email, write 'not stated' instead of guessing. It repeats identically because the format and the rule for missing data are both fixed, so nothing about the output depends on how the email happens to be worded - that's what a reviewer would check first if the output ever looked different twice.
List each claim on its own line - date, amount, category, submitter - then total the amount column at the bottom for the memo total.
The dates are wrong - the call was the 14th, and the 19th is five days later, not the three days out the email claims. I'd check the call log for the actual agreed date.

The 15% delivery increase is correct, not the issue. The on-time rate is wrong - 3 late out of 62 is about 95%, not 97%. And the 'held steady' stock figure, while it adds up on its own, is never explained against a 15% rise in deliveries that week. I'd check both against the depot's own records rather than the report's own numbers.
Output 2 - it shows the €612,000 and €25,100 that the 4.1% is worked out from, not just the bare percentage.
Reply 2, it has the order and credit references so both claims can be checked. Reply 1's 'entirely our error' isn't something you can verify yet, though it might turn out to be right.

The pricing and volume discounts are sensitive, so those wouldn't go in as they are. The confidentiality clause naming both parties makes me want to handle the whole thing carefully. The delivery schedule on its own seems low-risk to paste as is.
Before the weekly report is sent, I cross-check the totals against the source system, which would catch a wrong figure, not just a typo.

Step 4 needs the gate most, since the confirmation sends automatically and can't be pulled back. Step 1 also carries risk, since a bad read of the order feeds into everything after it - I'd have the gate flag anything with an unusual quantity or a borderline stock match.
